items.note: Author says Devapaladeva's inscriptions record that Iltutmish's posted chief at Vidisha was killed; Vidisha under Paramara control was no longer as before the attack.
items.gloss: The inscriptions of Devapaladeva tell that the mleccha chief posted by Iltutmish after plundering and ruining Vidisha was struck down. After coming under Paramara control Vidisha was no longer the same as when it was left after the attack.

items.note: Suggests Narayan Vyas called Udaypur a land of heroes because its ancestors saved the temple from Tughlaq's raiders a hundred years after Iltutmish; temple survived largely intact.
items.gloss: Narayan Vyas perhaps called Udaipur a land of heroes because Udaipur's ancestors saved the temple in its full height from being razed by the equally greedy raiders of Tughlaq, who came a hundred years after Iltutmish. Looking at ruined temples in this region it is a great miracle that the temple built by Raja Udayaditya survived largely.

claim.value: saved by ancestors' resistance against Tughlaq raiders (author, after Narayan Vyas)

items.note: Naravarman, son of Udayaditya and 13th Paramara king, built the grander Vijay temple at Vidisha, which lasted only a hundred years; the father's work still stands after a thousand.
items.gloss: As Vijay Mandir, Naravarman, son of Maharaj Udayaditya and the 13th king of the Paramara dynasty, made a bigger and grander construction than his father at Vidisha. But it survived only a hundred years. The great father's creation still stands proudly after a thousand years.

items.note: A hill-fort rampart built for emergencies sheltered Hindus who fled from all sides and could see the temple courtyard below.
items.gloss: Hindus who had come from all sides and hidden behind the hill fort's rampart, built for safety in emergencies, got brief relief there. They must have been watching from here the great noise rising from the temple courtyard below.

items.note: Failed wall built against the temple's rear west side; two doorways on north and south still stand with Tughlaq inscriptions.
items.gloss: In the temple courtyard you will see an unsuccessful attempt to raise a wall right against the rear western part of the temple. Two doorways were built on both sides of the temple, north and south. They stand to this day, and bear Tughlaq's inscriptions.

items.note: Author argues that the temple was not harmed later despite Khilji and Sher Shah Suri's rule; descendants of Paramaras or their subjects must have defended it (inference).
items.gloss: It means that despite coming under Malwa's Khiljis and Sher Shah Suri's raiders, the temple was not harmed in later periods. They must have shown power by building mosques from debris of ancient monuments near the palaces, away from the temple, but the descendants or subjects of the Paramaras must have left no stone unturned in defending Udaipur.

items.note: Author reads that, after the temple was seized, images were destroyed, the west gate was closed and a small prayer structure raised in six to eight months, and the western doorway built from debris of broken mandapas.
items.gloss: After the temple came into possession, its demolition began too, and in the first round every image inside and outside was being erased. The temple's west gate was closed and a small place of worship erected, a job of six to eight months. The west doorway leading into the temple was raised in the same period from rubble of mandapas broken in the temple complex.

items.note: Author conjectures armed local resistance drove occupiers out, leaving the wall unfinished.
items.gloss: Powerful local residents must have driven out those who occupied the temple complex by hard fighting, an armed struggle in which many warriors must have died but who finally succeeded. This event must have happened; otherwise the temple would not have survived. They fled leaving the wall unfinished or were killed.

claim.value: armed local resistance drove occupiers out (author's inference)

reject_reason: political commentary on independent India; no evidence

items.note: Chanderi Gate: an archaeology official said an old temple once stood there; image and pillar fragments lie neglected, and a tiny later mosque-like structure outside the gate uses temple debris.
items.gloss: We went to the Chanderi gate, about which an archaeology department officer had said an old temple must once have stood there. Pieces of images and pillars still lie orphaned. Just outside the gate is a tiny mosque-like structure of a later period, big enough for five people to pray, in which the temple debris itself is used.

items.note: Five or seven memorial tombs and several sati pillars around Chanderi Gate, hemmed in by houses and nearly vanishing.
items.gloss: Around it we saw five-seven samadhis hemmed in by houses and almost vanishing. Several sati pillars stood there, close to disappearing. Most of the surrounding population is Muslim. In coming years those pillars may be enclosed in their dense settlements and ended.

items.note: Four INTACH team members were measuring a dark cellar in the palace ruins, more than ten days into the work.
items.gloss: Dr Narayan Vyas went along to see the palace ruins where four members of the INTACH team were measuring a dark cellar below. Their work was in its final phase. They had been there for over ten days and were thrilled to be here.

items.note: Author says a government department spent Rs 76 lakh on two mosques while Udaypur's fresh ruin went on before its eyes.
items.gloss: The last sign of their existence too was being destroyed. This is the most painful picture of Udaipur's fresh ruin happening before the eyes of a government department that spent 76 lakh rupees on two mosques.

items.note: Udaysamudra: INTACH measured length 980 m; carved-stone ghat steps now descend into wheat fields on black soil; a foot's digging gave shells and a copper coin.
items.gloss: Before leaving Udaipur we went to Uday Samudra, where the INTACH team had worked a week earlier and measured its length as 980 metres. The steps of the splendid carved-stone ghats now descend not into Uday Samudra but into fields where wheat stood ready for harvest, a vast tank built by Udayaditya once lapped the shores like a sea. Digging a foot or so on the top surface gave many shells and a copper coin.

claim.value: tank built by Udayaditya, 980 m long (INTACH), now fields

items.note: Uday Samudra's carved stones likened to the large reservoirs near Bhojpur with stepped stone dams making Bhimkund.
items.gloss: The carved stones on the banks of Uday Samudra are like the huge reservoirs built on the way to Bhojpur in Bhopal: stepped stone dams that presented the sight of Bhimkund's surging sea in front of the Bhojpur temple.

items.note: Dam and reservoir building as Paramara expertise; reservoirs served caravans and town water supply; Udaypur has countless stepwells besides Udaysamudra.
items.gloss: Dam and reservoir building was a Paramara speciality. Wherever huge temples were built, even larger reservoirs were made. In the eight dry months they served as halting places for caravans of freight carriers, traders, sadhus, pilgrims, military groups and thousands of cattle. The town's water supply too. In Udaipur apart from Uday Samudra countless stepwells were built where Paramara craftsmen displayed their skill.

items.note: Reclining image at Uday Samudra believed a royal dancer, called Bedni Mata; local story that she was to dance on a thin thread tied across the reservoir, someone cut it, she fell and died; the image is her samadhi.
items.gloss: It is considered the image of a royal dancer, also called Bedni Mata. A popular story among locals about this sindoor-smeared image is that she was to dance on a thin thread tied across the reservoir. Once someone broke the thread and the dancer could not finish her dance. She died from the fall. This is her samadhi.

claim.value: royal dancer fell from a cut thread over the reservoir; image is her samadhi

items.note: Dr Narayan Vyas, after looking closely, said the image is a yaksha.
items.gloss: But Dr Narayan Vyas, after looking at the image carefully, told us on the way back that it is an image of a yaksha.

claim.value: Narayan Vyas: image is a yaksha

items.note: Author imagines the royal dancer awaiting the king's chariots at the flag-hoisting ceremony of 30 March 1080 on the temple's completion; Udaypur shone for another 250 years.
items.gloss: When the temple's construction was complete she may have waited for the king's chariots at the flag-hoisting ceremony of 30 March 1080. That splendour of Udaipur's palaces was not the last. Udaipur kept shining like this for another two and a half hundred years.

items.note: Author conjectures Udaypur stayed untouched during Iltutmish's and Khilji's attacks on Vidisha, its warriors perhaps repelling raiders alongside the Paramara army.
items.gloss: During Iltutmish's fierce attacks on Vidisha and Khilji's plunder, very bad news must have come to frighten Udaipur, but Udaipur remained untouched. Certainly in those attacks Udaipur's warriors must have clashed with the bands of these two raiders alongside the Paramara army and succeeded in saving their town.
